## Limitations

     Every study has limits. Identifying them honestly is a sign
     of scholarly rigor. Address at least THREE of the following:
       • Sample size and generalizability
       • Single coder reliability (you were the only coder)
       • Time period (results may not generalize beyond your window)
       • Archive coverage (what the archive may have missed)
       • Operationalization choices (how your definitions shaped results)
     ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── -->

Several limitations of the present study should be noted. First, [LIMITATION 1 — e.g., "the sample was drawn from a single archive, which may not capture the full range of coverage available across all relevant outlets and platforms"]. Second, [LIMITATION 2 — e.g., "all coding was conducted by a single coder, which precludes the calculation of inter-rater reliability. Future studies should employ at least two independent coders and report Cohen's Kappa or Krippendorff's Alpha"]. Third, [LIMITATION 3 — e.g., "the study period of [DATE RANGE] may reflect idiosyncratic coverage patterns tied to [SPECIFIC EVENT], limiting the generalizability of findings to other time periods"]. [Add a fourth limitation if relevant.]

These limitations notwithstanding, the study's systematic sampling procedure, pre-registered codebook, and use of inferential statistics represent meaningful methodological strengths that support the credibility of the findings.
